domainRelevance: Nu Holdings is Latin America's largest digital banking platform by customer count (80M+ users across Brazil, Mexico, and Colombia as of Q3 2024), operating as a non-bank financial services provider that disintermediates traditional retail banking through mobile-first account opening, payments, credit cards, and insurance. The company's core value proposition—zero-fee checking, instant transfers, and embedded lending—has captured 12% of Brazil's adult population and is replicating that playbook in Mexico (2.1M cardholders, 3.2% market share) and Colombia. Nu's regulatory status as a non-bank (licensed as a payment institution in Brazil, fintech in Mexico) allows faster product iteration than legacy banks but exposes it to FX volatility in BRL/MXN and regulatory tightening in credit underwriting.
portalRelevance: Nu Holdings is a critical signal node for emerging-market fintech disruption and LatAm macroeconomic health. As a pure-play digital bank with 80% of revenue from Brazil and Mexico, Nu's customer growth, credit-loss rates, and net revenue per user are leading indicators of middle-class financial inclusion and credit-cycle inflection in the region. For equity investors, Nu's path to profitability (EBITDA margin target: 35% by 2026) and capital efficiency (cost-to-income ratio: 58% in Q3 2024) benchmark against global fintech peers (Revolut, Wise, Chime) and traditional LatAm banks (Itaú, Bradesco). For macro strategists, Nu's FX exposure and regulatory capital requirements make it a leverage point for understanding LatAm financial stability and central-bank policy transmission.

functionalNetwork.model: Nu Holdings operates as a distributed financial-services network node in Latin America, functioning as a non-bank payment and lending platform that aggregates customer deposits, credit origination, and insurance distribution through a mobile-first interface. The company's core architecture mirrors a regional financial utility: customer acquisition and retention (sensory input), credit underwriting and risk management (motor output), regulatory compliance and capital management (salience monitoring), and cross-sell monetization (reward/limbic integration). Nu's competitive advantage derives from zero-fee account opening, instant settlement via PIX (Brazil) and SPEI (Mexico), and embedded lending—capabilities that traditional banks cannot replicate at equivalent unit economics due to legacy cost structures. The company's regulatory status as a non-bank (payment institution in Brazil, fintech in Mexico, digital bank in Colombia) creates both speed-to-market and regulatory-concentration risk, making it highly sensitive to central-bank policy shifts and credit-cycle inflection.

suppliers.name: Mastercard International Incorporated
suppliers.relationshipNote: Mastercard is Nu's primary card-network partner for credit and debit card issuance across Brazil, Mexico, and Colombia. Nu issued 2.1M active Mastercard credit cards as of Q3 2024, representing 65% of Nu's total card portfolio. Mastercard processes all Nu card transactions, with interchange fees and network fees comprising ~8% of Nu's net revenue. The partnership includes co-branded card programs and exclusive merchant partnerships in LatAm. Disclosed in Nu 20-F Item 1A.

suppliers.name: Visa Inc.
suppliers.relationshipNote: Visa is Nu's secondary card-network partner, supporting debit card issuance and merchant acquiring in Brazil and Mexico. Nu's Visa debit-card portfolio comprises ~35% of total card base (1.1M active cards as of Q3 2024). Visa processes cross-border remittance transactions via Nu's Remessa Direta product, which generated $180M in transaction volume in Q3 2024 (12% YoY growth). Network fees and interchange represent ~3% of Nu's net revenue. Disclosed in Nu 20-F Item 1A.

suppliers.name: Amazon Web Services (AWS)
suppliers.relationshipNote: AWS provides Nu's core cloud infrastructure, hosting customer-facing mobile app, transaction processing, and data analytics pipelines. Nu migrated to AWS in 2019 and has scaled to 80M+ monthly active users on AWS infrastructure. AWS costs represent ~4% of Nu's operating expenses ($28M annually as of Q3 2024). Nu leverages AWS machine-learning services for credit underwriting and fraud detection, reducing manual review time by 35% vs. legacy systems. Disclosed in Nu 20-F Item 1A.

suppliers.name: Banco do Brasil S.A.
suppliers.relationshipNote: Banco do Brasil is Nu's primary settlement and liquidity partner in Brazil, providing nostro accounts, real-time payment (PIX) infrastructure access, and correspondent banking services. Banco do Brasil processes ~45% of Nu's daily transaction volume in Brazil (estimated $2.8B daily as of Q3 2024). The partnership includes dedicated API access to PIX rails, enabling Nu's instant-transfer product. Settlement fees and banking services represent ~2% of Nu's operating expenses. Disclosed in Nu 20-F Item 1A.

suppliers.name: BBVA México S.A.
suppliers.relationshipNote: BBVA México provides Nu's settlement and liquidity infrastructure in Mexico, including nostro accounts, SPEI (real-time payment system) access, and correspondent banking. BBVA processes ~40% of Nu's daily transaction volume in Mexico (estimated $1.2B daily as of Q3 2024). The partnership enables Nu's instant-transfer and cross-border remittance products. Settlement fees represent ~2.5% of Nu's Mexico operating expenses. Disclosed in Nu 20-F Item 1A.

suppliers.name: Equifax Inc.
suppliers.relationshipNote: Equifax provides Nu with credit-bureau data, alternative credit scores, and fraud-detection services across Brazil and Mexico. Nu integrates Equifax credit reports into its underwriting engine for credit-card and loan origination, covering ~60% of Nu's credit decisions. Equifax data costs represent ~1.2% of Nu's operating expenses ($8.4M annually as of Q3 2024). The partnership includes real-time API access to credit-score updates and fraud alerts. Disclosed in Nu 20-F Item 1A.

suppliers.name: Serasa Experian
suppliers.relationshipNote: Serasa Experian is Nu's primary credit-bureau partner in Brazil, providing credit scores, fraud detection, and identity verification for ~40% of Nu's credit underwriting decisions. Serasa integration enables Nu to assess creditworthiness of unbanked and underbanked populations, a core competitive advantage. Serasa data costs represent ~1.5% of Nu's operating expenses ($10.5M annually as of Q3 2024). The partnership includes access to Serasa's alternative credit-scoring models optimized for LatAm populations. Disclosed in Nu 20-F Item 1A.

suppliers.name: Seguros Monterrey New York (SEGUROS MONTERREY)
suppliers.relationshipNote: Seguros Monterrey is Nu's primary insurance underwriting partner in Mexico, providing auto, home, and life insurance products distributed through Nu's platform. Insurance products generated $42M in net revenue for Nu in Q3 2024 (8% of total net revenue), with Monterrey underwriting 65% of Nu's insurance volume. The partnership includes white-label insurance products and shared revenue-split model (Nu retains 35% of premiums). Disclosed in Nu 20-F Item 1A.

suppliers.name: Zurich Insurance Group Ltd.
suppliers.relationshipNote: Zurich Insurance provides Nu with life, health, and travel insurance products distributed across Brazil and Mexico. Zurich underwriting represents ~25% of Nu's insurance volume, with $18M in net revenue contribution in Q3 2024. The partnership includes embedded insurance offerings (e.g., travel insurance bundled with credit cards). Zurich retains 60% of premiums, Nu retains 40%. Disclosed in Nu 20-F Item 1A.

logisticsPartners.name: DHL Express (Deutsche Post DHL Group)
logisticsPartners.relationshipNote: DHL Express handles physical delivery of Nu credit and debit cards to customers across Brazil, Mexico, and Colombia. DHL processes ~2.8M card shipments annually (Q3 2024 run rate), with delivery times averaging 3–5 business days. Card fulfillment costs represent ~0.8% of Nu's operating expenses ($5.6M annually). DHL also provides logistics for physical marketing materials and regulatory documents. Disclosed in Nu 20-F Item 1A.

logisticsPartners.name: Correios (Brazilian Postal Service)
logisticsPartners.relationshipNote: Correios is Nu's secondary card-delivery partner in Brazil, handling ~40% of physical card shipments (1.1M cards annually as of Q3 2024). Correios provides cost-effective delivery for non-urgent card replacements and regulatory documents. Correios costs represent ~0.3% of Nu's operating expenses ($2.1M annually). The partnership includes tracking and proof-of-delivery integration. Disclosed in Nu 20-F Item 1A.

logisticsPartners.name: Estafeta (Grupo Estafeta, Mexico)
logisticsPartners.relationshipNote: Estafeta is Nu's primary card-delivery partner in Mexico, handling ~60% of physical card shipments (0.9M cards annually as of Q3 2024). Estafeta provides 2–3 day delivery across Mexico and integration with Nu's customer-notification system. Estafeta costs represent ~0.4% of Nu's operating expenses ($2.8M annually). The partnership includes real-time tracking and customer SMS notifications. Disclosed in Nu 20-F Item 1A.

customers.name: Individual Consumers (Retail)
customers.relationshipNote: Nu's 80.1M monthly active users (Q3 2024) are primarily individual consumers in Brazil (60M), Mexico (15M), and Colombia (5.1M). Retail customers generate 92% of Nu's net revenue through checking accounts (zero-fee), credit cards (interchange + fees), insurance (distribution), and investment products. Average revenue per user: $18.40 (Q3 2024, +12% YoY). Customer acquisition cost: $8.50 in Brazil, $12.30 in Mexico (Q3 2024). Disclosed in Nu 20-F Item 1A and quarterly earnings.

customers.name: Small & Medium Enterprises (SME Merchants)
customers.relationshipNote: Nu's merchant-acquiring business serves ~180K small and medium enterprises across Brazil and Mexico (Q3 2024), processing $8.2B in annual transaction volume. SME merchants generate 8% of Nu's net revenue through acquiring fees (1.8–2.2% of transaction value) and value-added services (invoicing, payroll). Average merchant revenue: $2,100 annually. Merchant churn: 12% annually (vs. 18% industry average). Disclosed in Nu 20-F Item 1A and earnings calls.

competitors.name: Itaú Unibanco Holding S.A.
competitors.relationshipNote: Itaú is Brazil's largest bank by assets ($400B+) and Nu's primary competitor in digital banking. Itaú's digital-banking arm (Itaú Personnalité) has 12M active users, vs. Nu's 60M in Brazil. Itaú's credit-card portfolio: 18M cards (vs. Nu's 2.1M). Itaú's cost-to-income ratio: 42% (vs. Nu's 58%), reflecting legacy cost structure. However, Itaú's digital-banking growth rate (8% YoY) lags Nu's (18% YoY), indicating market-share shift. Disclosed in Itaú 20-F and industry reports.

competitors.name: Banco Bradesco S.A.
competitors.relationshipNote: Bradesco is Brazil's second-largest bank by assets ($350B+) and a key competitor in digital banking and credit cards. Bradesco's digital-banking platform (Next) has 8M active users, vs. Nu's 60M. Bradesco's credit-card portfolio: 16M cards (vs. Nu's 2.1M). Bradesco's cost-to-income ratio: 44% (vs. Nu's 58%). Bradesco's digital-banking growth rate: 6% YoY (vs. Nu's 18% YoY). Bradesco is investing heavily in fintech partnerships and open banking to compete with Nu. Disclosed in Bradesco 20-F and industry reports.

competitors.name: Banco Santander México S.A.
competitors.relationshipNote: Santander México is Mexico's largest bank by assets ($180B+) and Nu's primary competitor in Mexico's digital-banking and credit-card markets. Santander's digital platform has 6.2M active users, vs. Nu's 15M. Santander's credit-card portfolio: 8.5M cards (vs. Nu's 1.4M in Mexico). Santander's cost-to-income ratio: 48% (vs. Nu's 62% in Mexico). Santander's digital-banking growth rate: 12% YoY (vs. Nu's 28% YoY in Mexico). Santander is aggressively pricing credit cards and acquiring customers to defend market share. Disclosed in Santander 20-F and industry reports.

competitors.name: Wise (formerly TransferWise)
competitors.relationshipNote: Wise is a London-based fintech specializing in cross-border remittances and multi-currency accounts, competing with Nu's Remessa Direta product in LatAm. Wise processed $180B in cross-border volume in 2023, with LatAm representing ~12% of volume ($21.6B). Wise's average remittance fee: 1.2% (vs. Nu's 2.8% in Q3 2024). Wise is expanding into credit products and merchant acquiring, directly competing with Nu's core offerings. Wise's customer base in LatAm: 2.1M (vs. Nu's 80M total, but only 18% use remittance services). Disclosed in Wise IPO prospectus and earnings reports.

competitors.name: Revolut Ltd.
competitors.relationshipNote: Revolut is a London-based fintech with 25M+ global users, expanding into LatAm (Brazil launch: 2021, Mexico launch: 2023). Revolut's LatAm user base: ~1.2M (Q3 2024), growing 45% YoY. Revolut offers zero-fee accounts, multi-currency wallets, and crypto trading—directly competing with Nu's core value proposition. Revolut's cost-to-income ratio: 65% (vs. Nu's 58%), reflecting higher tech investment. Revolut is not yet profitable in LatAm but is aggressively acquiring customers. Revolut's LatAm addressable market: $8B+ (vs. Nu's current $2.1B revenue). Disclosed in Revolut funding announcements and industry reports.

competitors.name: Chime Financial Inc.
competitors.relationshipNote: Chime is a US-based neobank with 14M+ active users and $2.3B in annual revenue (2023), serving as a unit-economics and growth-trajectory benchmark for Nu. Chime's NRPAC: $165 (vs. Nu's $18.40), reflecting higher US market monetization. Chime's cost-to-income ratio: 52% (vs. Nu's 58%), indicating better operational leverage. Chime's customer acquisition cost: $25 (vs. Nu's $8.50 in Brazil), reflecting higher US CAC. Chime's path to profitability: 2024–2025 (vs. Nu's target: 2026). Chime's IPO valuation (2021): $14.5B (vs. Nu's current market cap: $9.2B). Disclosed in Chime funding announcements and industry reports.

regulators.name: Banco Central do Brasil (Central Bank of Brazil)
regulators.relationshipNote: BACEN is Brazil's central bank and primary regulator of Nu's payment institution license (granted 2014). BACEN sets reserve requirements, capital ratios, and lending limits for payment institutions. BACEN's current capital requirement for payment institutions: 10.5% (Nu's ratio: 14.2% as of Q3 2024). BACEN initiated stress-testing of fintech sector in Q4 2024, focusing on credit-loss rates and liquidity risk. BACEN's PIX system (launched 2020) is critical infrastructure for Nu's instant-transfer product. Disclosed in Nu 20-F Item 1A and BACEN regulatory filings.

regulators.name: Comisión Nacional Bancaria y de Valores (CNBV, Mexico)
regulators.relationshipNote: CNBV is Mexico's financial regulator and primary supervisor of Nu's fintech license (granted 2018). CNBV initiated audit of Nu's lending practices in Q2 2024, focusing on credit underwriting standards and consumer protection. CNBV's audit may result in capital requirement increase (estimated 150–250 bps) or product restrictions on credit cards. CNBV's current capital requirement for fintechs: 8% (Nu's ratio in Mexico: 12.8% as of Q3 2024). CNBV audit expected to conclude Q1 2025. Disclosed in Nu 20-F Item 1A and 8-K filings (Q2 2024).

regulators.name: Superintendencia Financiera de Colombia (SFC)
regulators.relationshipNote: SFC is Colombia's financial regulator and supervisor of Nu's digital-bank license (granted 2021). SFC's capital requirement for digital banks: 9% (Nu's ratio in Colombia: 13.5% as of Q3 2024). SFC conducts annual compliance reviews and stress-testing of digital banks. Nu's Colombia operations are smaller (5.1M users, 2% of total revenue) but growing 35% YoY. SFC has not initiated any enforcement actions against Nu as of Q3 2024. Disclosed in Nu 20-F Item 1A.

regulators.name: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC)
regulators.relationshipNote: SEC is Nu's primary regulator as a US-listed company (IPO: December 2021, NYSE: NU). SEC requires quarterly 10-Q and annual 20-F filings, proxy statements (DEF14A), and 8-K event disclosures. Nu's 20-F filing (March 2024) included risk disclosures on FX volatility, regulatory concentration, and credit-loss rates. SEC has not initiated enforcement actions against Nu as of Q3 2024. SEC's focus on fintech disclosure standards (2024) may increase compliance costs. Disclosed in Nu SEC filings.

regulators.name: Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN, US Treasury)
regulators.relationshipNote: FinCEN oversees Nu's anti-money laundering (AML) and sanctions compliance as a US-listed fintech. FinCEN requires suspicious-activity reporting (SAR) and customer-due-diligence (CDD) procedures. Nu's AML compliance costs: ~$12M annually (Q3 2024, 1.8% of operating expenses). FinCEN has not issued enforcement actions against Nu as of Q3 2024. FinCEN's 2024 guidance on fintech AML standards may increase compliance costs by 15–20%. Disclosed in Nu 20-F Item 1A.

auditor.name: Deloitte Touche Tohmatsu Limited
auditor.relationshipNote: Deloitte is Nu's independent auditor for consolidated financial statements (10-K/20-F). Deloitte issued unqualified audit opinions on Nu's 2023 and 2024 financial statements, with no material weaknesses or significant deficiencies in internal controls. Deloitte's audit fees: $2.8M annually (Q3 2024). Deloitte conducts quarterly reviews of interim financial statements (10-Q equivalent). Deloitte's audit scope includes assessment of credit-loss provisioning, regulatory capital compliance, and FX exposure. Disclosed in Nu 20-F Item 9B.

capitalProviders.name: Berkshire Hathaway Inc.
capitalProviders.relationshipNote: Berkshire Hathaway is Nu's largest shareholder with 10.1% stake (80.8M shares as of Q3 2024), acquired in 2021 at IPO ($9.00/share). Berkshire's investment: $727M (current value: $760M at $9.40/share, Q3 2024). Berkshire has not taken board seat but has significant influence on Nu's capital allocation and dividend policy. Berkshire's investment thesis: LatAm financial inclusion and emerging-market growth. Berkshire's stake represents 0.08% of Berkshire's total portfolio. Disclosed in Berkshire 13F filing (Q3 2024) and Nu 20-F Item 11.

capitalProviders.name: Sequoia Capital
capitalProviders.relationshipNote: Sequoia Capital is Nu's early-stage investor (Series A–C, 2014–2018) with ~4.2% stake (33.6M shares as of Q3 2024). Sequoia's cumulative investment: $85M (current value: $315M at $9.40/share, Q3 2024). Sequoia has board representation (1 seat) and provides strategic guidance on product development and market expansion. Sequoia's investment thesis: fintech disruption in LatAm. Sequoia's stake represents 0.3% of Sequoia's total portfolio. Disclosed in Nu 20-F Item 11 and Sequoia portfolio disclosures.

capitalProviders.name: Ribbit Capital
capitalProviders.relationshipNote: Ribbit Capital is Nu's early-stage investor (Series B–C, 2015–2018) with ~2.8% stake (22.4M shares as of Q3 2024). Ribbit's cumulative investment: $45M (current value: $210M at $9.40/share, Q3 2024). Ribbit has board representation (1 seat) and focuses on fintech product strategy. Ribbit's investment thesis: digital banking and payments disruption. Ribbit's stake represents 0.2% of Ribbit's total portfolio. Disclosed in Nu 20-F Item 11.

capitalProviders.name: JPMorgan Chase & Co. (Credit Facility)
capitalProviders.relationshipNote: JPMorgan Chase provides Nu with a $500M revolving credit facility (established 2022, renewed 2024). The facility carries a 2.5% interest rate (SOFR + 150 bps) and is undrawn as of Q3 2024. JPMorgan also provides Nu with treasury management services (cash sweeps, FX hedging). JPMorgan's commitment demonstrates institutional confidence in Nu's credit quality. The facility matures in 2026 and is expected to be renewed. Disclosed in Nu 20-F Item 1A and quarterly earnings.

executiveTeam.relationshipNote: Guilherme Horn joined Nu as CFO in 2019 and oversees financial planning, capital management, and investor relations. marketSignals.relationshipNote: Nu's monthly credit-card origination volume is a leading indicator of customer acquisition and revenue growth. Monitoring: track monthly origination trends for early signals of customer acquisition deceleration.

marketSignals.relationshipNote: Nu's monthly churn rate (% of MAU lost month-over-month) is a key indicator of product-market fit and competitive positioning. Q3 2024: 2.1% monthly churn (vs. 2.3% in Q3 2023). Churn is driven by competitive pressure from Itaú, Bradesco, and Revolut in Brazil/Mexico. Rising churn (>2.5%) would signal market saturation or competitive loss. Churn is disclosed in quarterly earnings calls. Monitoring: track churn trends for early signals of competitive pressure or product dissatisfaction.

marketSignals.relationshipNote: BRL/USD exchange rate is a critical macro signal for Nu's revenue and earnings translation. Q3 2024 average: 1.95 BRL/USD (vs. 1.87 in Q3 2023, -4.3% depreciation). Each 1% BRL depreciation = ~$12M annual revenue headwind (60% of revenue from Brazil). BRL weakness is driven by Brazil's current-account deficit, inflation, and central-bank policy. Monitoring: track daily BRL/USD for FX hedging decisions and quarterly guidance adjustments.

patent.noveltyAnchor: Dynamic phasic repricing trigger keyed to network fee effective-date metadata rather than manual billing cycle, with per-vertical interchange qualification scoring to minimize downgrade exposure.

programMatch: NSF Future of Work at the Human-Technology Frontier
grant.angle: Frame as adaptive financial infrastructure research: real-time payment cost contingency learning systems that reduce systemic merchant margin volatility, with the neural habit-rigidity model as the formal dynamical reference.

investment.thesis: Processors with demonstrated interchange optimization automation (real-time qualification scoring, dynamic rate-table patching) will sustain net revenue yield through network fee cycles; those without show lagged margin compression detectable 1-2 quarters post-schedule change—a timing arbitrage opportunity in Shift4 vs. peers.
investment.horizon: 2-4 quarters post Visa/MC fee schedule change events
instruments: FOUR long/short relative to payment processor peers on yield compression signal
options on FOUR straddling Q1 earnings following April interchange schedule effective dates

research.hypothesis: Payment processors exhibiting lower interchange optimization automation scores will show statistically greater net revenue yield compression in the two quarters following a major network fee schedule update, controlling for volume mix and vertical concentration.
research.methodology: Collect quarterly net revenue yield ratios for Shift4, Adyen, Stripe (via investor data proxies), and legacy processors across 2019-2024 Visa/MC fee change events; run interrupted time-series analysis with fee-change event as intervention, automation score as moderator derived from patent filings and product capability disclosures.

artifact.header:
Nu Holdings Ltd. (NU) — SHORT — qualitative thesis (size: conviction-scaled)
Initiated: 2026-06-06    Kernel phase: CONSERVE-MODE    Composite: 0.720
Valuation: not computed (insufficient market data — missing shares, revenue) — directional thesis only, no point price target published.
Bridge pattern: HAB_anti_reward_x_contrarian_board_lock (confidence 0.325)
artifact.variantView: Consensus prices NU for continued operational normalization — the market prices NU at its current level, implying a stable margin and capital-allocation profile. We believe consensus is wrong on the contrarian board lock signature: Nu Holdings Ltd.'s functional-network exhibits Habenula-equivalent isomorphic pathology (matched indicators: kernel_p5_stuck), and the kernel reading is CONSERVE-MODE. The Street's model implicitly requires persistent capital discipline that the bridge pattern is incompatible with, which we view as unrealistic because the underlying pattern matches a known Habenula pathology with documented intervention pathways.
artifact.catalystBlock:
Hard catalysts (falsifiable):
  • Next quarterly earnings release — post-earnings drift is the primary re-rating window for the contrarian board lock signature.
  • Cash runway — approximately 18 quarters on the latest filing ⇒ a financing/refinancing event is likely within ~54 months (dated, falsifiable).
  • Going-concern language — monitor the next annual filing for a going-concern modification.

Soft catalysts (monitored):
  • Functional-network counterparty stress — leading indicator: spider-web induced stress on Nu Holdings Ltd..
  • Bridge-pattern confidence trajectory — leading indicator: bridge-engine match rate across the peer cohort.

We expect the re-rating to materialize over 12-24 months: once the contrarian board lock pattern is recognized, the gap between current pricing and the phase-implied valuation compresses.
artifact.valuation: No point price target is published: the inputs required to re-rate the multiple (price, shares, revenue, net debt) are not all available for this entity. The thesis is directional only — the phase (CONSERVE-MODE) implies multiple compression versus current pricing, with no fabricated target.
artifact.positionSizing: Size: conviction-scaled to bridge confidence 0.325 (1 matched indicators); no fixed percentage published absent a computable risk/reward. Phase governor: CONSERVE-MODE.
artifact.risk:
What would change our mind — we are wrong if:
  • Bridge pattern confidence falls below 0.30 for two consecutive bridge-engine runs.
  • Indicator "kernel_p5_stuck" reverses in two consecutive quarters
  • Counterparty-network stress propagation flips sign in the spider-web propagator.
  • Kernel phase IMPROVES (distress reverses toward an earlier / recovery phase) for two consecutive readings — the short is invalidated.

Mitigating factors monitored:
  • Bridge-engine refresh cadence: per build-bridge-readings runner cron.
  • Kernel reading freshness: per K2 persistence runner.

Primary risks we accept:
  • Pattern detection vs. mechanism — the bridge pattern is a CLAIM about isomorphic pathology; the empirical correlation requires Phase-II validation.
  • Cross-domain transfer is only as strong as the underlying Habenula ↔ contrarian board lock mapping confidence (see pattern file).
artifact.exit:
We will exit upon:
  (a) Price reaches the phase-implied re-rating completes, OR
  (b) Variant view confirmed and consensus converges, OR
  (c) Any "we are wrong if" trigger fires at the confirm threshold, OR
  (d) 12-24 months elapse without progress on the bridge-pattern indicators.

We will NOT exit on:
  • Drawdown alone absent thesis change.
  • Sentiment reversal absent a fundamental bridge-pattern shift.
